---
title: "Working with class imbalance"
date-modified: "2025-04-28"
---

Datasets NSOs need to classify are typically not equally distributed, as
some classes have many records (i.e. unique products) while others have
only a few. This requires additional steps to be taken when designing
and testing classifiers. Specitically, this represents a challenge for
automated methods (such as [Method 4 or Machine Learning
(ML)](method-4-machine-learning-classification-method.qmd)), as models could struggle when they don\'t have a
lot of examples to learn from, thus typically misclassifying sparse
categories. This chapter introduces approaches that NSOs could use to
mitigate consequences that arise from such class imbalance problems.

# Overview of the problem {#Workingwithclassimbalance-Overviewoftheproblem}

An imbalanced class distribution is a case where class sizes within a
dataset vary significantly in size amongst each other. In the context of
the alternative data training data sets, imbalanced data or (mulit)class
imbalances means that there are some classes - the majority classes -
for which we find plenty examples in the data (e. g. red wine) while
other classes  - the minority classes - are represented by barely a few
articles (e. g. bananas). This presents a challenge for supervised ML
models, which typically work well when the number of samples in each
class are about equal. This is because most algorithms are designed to
optimize based on a cost function. However, if the data set is highly
imbalanced, a model could minimize the cost function at the expense of
minority classes. This implies an indirect weighting of the majority
classes by overrepresentation. The model may also not learn to easily
distinguish a class from another if there are not enough examples. As a
result, some classes could be systematically misclassified while the
overall score for the classifier with many classes could be relatively
high ([for instance micro F1
scores](how-to-evaluate-classification-methods.qmd)). This is
a challenge within price statistics as classification is a critical step
prior to applying price index formulas on each [retailer, category, and
geography combination in order to determine the sub-elementary aggregate
index](aggregation.qmd). Misclassification may thus cause
bias in the calculated index that may also impact the elementary
aggregate this data is integrated into (1).

# Distribution test {#Workingwithclassimbalance-Distributiontest}

Prior to any actions to deal with class imbalance during model training
(more on options below), the first thing NSOs could do to understand if
the dataset is imbalanced, especially if it is not immediately obvious.
A dataset is imbalanced when the classes are not approximately equally
distributed. A test statistic can be adopted to check for the
balance(dness) of a dataset. For this purpose the following null
hypothesis is used:

**H0:** The distribution of the underlying dataset follows a uniform
distribution

To test that hypothesis, the [Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS)
test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmogorov%E2%80%93Smirnov_test)
could be used. In general, the KS test checks whether two empirical
distribution functions correspond to each other (2).

In the present case, the procedure is as follows:

1.  A hypothetical (reference) distribution function is considered.
    Corresponding to the null hypothesis, a uniform distribution is
    considered.
2.  The frequency of each class (COICOP) is determined and assorted in
    an ascending order.
3.  Then, the empirical distribution function is determined. This
    includes the distribution parameters - the support parameters
    (a,b) - which are necessary to create the hypothesized uniform
    distribution.
4.  The empirical distribution function is then compared with the
    hypothetical distribution function. Here, the cumulative density
    function (CDF) is calculated in each case and the function value at
    arbitrary chosen points are compared.
5.  If the CDFs are approximately equal, the H0 can\'t be rejected.

Note, the KS test is applicable to test for any distribution.

# Resampling techniques {#Workingwithclassimbalance-Resamplingtechniques}

Several techniques are widely used to address class imbalance. One is to
assign distinct costs to training examples, and the other resampling.
Among resampling, two approaches are used: undersamping, where labels
from the majority class in the dataset are removed in order to balance
the data; and oversampling, where more examples are added to the
minority classes of the data. Resampling approaches are summarized in
more detail below.

## Undersampling {#Workingwithclassimbalance-Undersampling}

Undersampling techniques aim to balance class distributions by
[minimizing]{.underline} majority class items. This can be done randomly
or according to more sophisticated concepts. Tomek links for instance is
one such commonly used sophisticated approach that finds and removes
noisy and hard to classify observations to help find a more disrable
decision boundary (see [imbalanced learn site for more
guidance](https://imbalanced-learn.org/dev/under_sampling.html#tomek-s-links)).
An undersampled dataset posses the advantage that it is more balanced
among the classes/labels and that it may help to improve storage
problems and runtime, especially when the training data set is huge. It
has been proposed as good means of increasing the sensitivity of a
classifier to the minority class. On the other hand, it is very likely
that it discards potentially useful information in the data which can be
important for building classifiers. In addition, the undersampled
dataset can be biased in the sense that it is not an appropriate
representative of the population.

## Oversampling {#Workingwithclassimbalance-Oversampling}

An alternative is to oversample minority classes, which may be more
appropriate for NSOs. Specifically, as minority classes in alternative
datasets may be mostly represented by just a few items, undersampling
would be inappropriate as a balanced training dataset can only be
achieved by a huge loss of data, and thus a resultant compromise in the
quality of the ML classification. Oversampling techniques aim to balance
class distributions by [adding]{.underline} items to the minority class.
Thus, it is a good choice when the training data set does not possess
enough data in each class. The minority classes are not necessarily
supplemented by creating exact copies of the particular records in those
classes, as more diverse synthetic samples can also be created by
introducing small variations of the items. This rebalancing method has
is advantageous in that no information is lost, however its overuse can
increases the likelihood of an ML model overfitting through replication
of parts of the minority class specific items. 

Random Oversampling

The simplest oversampling technique refers to random oversampling. It
randomly selects examples from the minority class and adds them to the
training data set until an approximately balanced set is achieved. This
method is also applicable to the minority class\' feature space. As an
example, if ngrams are used for text classification, one can randomly
draw and combine ngrams from the minority class and add the result to
the training data set. It worth mentioning, that this approach increases
the likelihood of overfitting since examples or features are merely
duplicated and the feature space is not increased. NSOs may need to
regularize more heavily in this case to make sure models generalize out
of sample.

### SMOTE {#Workingwithclassimbalance-SMOTE}

In contrast to random oversampling with replacement, which does not
necessarily increase the recognition of the minority classes, Synthetic
Minority Oversampling Technique (or SMOTE) tries to identify similar but
more specific regions in the feature space for the minority classes. In
other words, the minority classes are oversampled by synthetically
creating new examples:

- *First*, features of the minority class are chosen (green points in
  panel a of Figure 1).
- *Second*, identify the *k* nearest neighbors (the black point in panel
  b of Figure 1 is a selected feature and whereas the yellow points
  represent its neighbors). One can determine the specific number of
  neighbors *k* arbitrarily or by using heuristics, such as the \"elbow
  method\".
- *Third*, synthetic examples are generated. Intuitively, this is done
  by randomly placing a point between the selected samples and their
  neighbors (red point between the brown points in panel c of Figure 1).
  Technically, the difference of the minority class feature vector and
  its nearest neighbor is taken. Thereafter, the differences are
  multiplied by a random number between 0 and 1. The resulting vector of
  synthetic features is added to the minority class\' feature vector. In
  the multiclass case, this procedure is repeated for each minority
  class.

Figure 1: How synthetic samples are generated with SMOTE. Each point
represent a record in the feature space. See Schubach et al (2017) for
more details.

![](images/working-with-class-imbalance/337281208.png)

Note, that SMOTE does not inherently consider feature relationships
beyond simple interpolation. It assumes that linear interpolation within
the minority class is safe and realistic, which may not always be the
case. The method also assumes features are independent or loosely
correlated, which is often not realistic in complex datasets. Thus, it
is important to consider the nature of the relationship between features
when generating synthetic data.

# Blended Sampling {#Workingwithclassimbalance-BlendedSampling}

NSOs can also apply a combination of oversampling the minority class and
undersampling the majority class can be useful to handle strongly
imbalanced data.
